2026-08-05.title: Stochastic Choice with Advertising
2026-08-05.abstract: We study how advertised products (e.g., “Top Picks,” “Recommended,” “Featured”) affect consumer choice on digital platforms and retail interfaces by extending the Luce (1959) (or multinomial logit) model. A consumer either focuses on the advertised items or considers the full menu, then chooses among the considered alternatives according to the Luce/logit rule. We characterize this model and show that its underlying primitives are uniquely identified from choice data. We also study a managerially important advertisement-design problem, in which a platform or retailer chooses the advertised subset to maximize expected profit, and we derive implementable design rules. We then introduce a richer framework in which advertising can influence both attention and preference. For this more general model, we provide a characterization and show how choice data can be used to separate the attention effect from the preference effect.
2026-08-05.introduction:
Consider a consumer who is searching online to hire a car in a popular destination. After entering the desired dates and location, many platforms display a selection of advertised listings, often labeled as “Top Picks,” “Recommended Choices,” or “Ideal for You.” These advertised listings are likely to influence their decision-making process. It is possible that they are drawn to the advertisements and limit their consideration to the advertised options; it is also possible that they still evaluate all available options.

The idea that an individual’s decision procedure is influenced by advertising is not new. A plethoric literature in economics, marketing, and psychology argues that advertising affects the choice process of a decision maker (DM).111For surveys on advertising in economics, marketing and psychology, see e.g. Bagwell (2007), Renault (2015), Fennis and Stroebe (2020) respectively. To investigate the role of advertisements in consumer choice, we develop the Luce model with Advertisement (LMA), which is a disciplined, minimal departure from the Luce rule tailored to settings where advertised alternatives are observable. Like the motivating example at the beginning, we posit that the advertisement takes the form of a set of advertised alternatives.222Many marketing studies examine this form of advertising, e.g. Mitra (1995), Shapiro, MacInnis, and Heckler (1997), Johnson, Lewis, and Reiley (2017), Melessa and Larsen (2024). For example, an advertisement can be a set of products advertised on billboards; or a set of “Amazon’s Picks”, “Sponsored Products”, “Best Sellers” on e-commerce platforms; or a set of products introduced on TV. We impose a set-directed attention rule: sometimes the consumer restricts attention to the advertised items available in the menu; sometimes they consider the full menu. Given the set of alternatives that the consumer pays attention to, they then make their choice based on the Luce rule.

The LMA framework speaks to a managerial question that is central for retailers and online platforms: which products should be advertised? Because many common digital advertising formats (such as “Top Picks,” “Recommended,” or “Featured” slots) primarily reallocate limited on-screen space rather than requiring substantial additional spending, improving the design of these advertisements may yield significant profit gains at relatively low cost. This issue is economically important in modern digital markets, where U.S. internet display advertising revenue alone reached 74.8 billion dollars in 2024.333Display advertising includes Banner, Rich Media, Sponsorship and Native advertising, of which Native advertising is exactly the type of advertising in our model. Manchanda et al. (2006) study effect of banner advertisement on internet purchasing. Source: IAB/PwC Internet Advertising Revenue Report 2024, accessible at https://www.iab.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/IAB_PwC-Internet-Ad-Revenue-Report-Full-Year-2024.pdf. This implies that even small improvements in the design of the advertised set can have large profit consequences. Yet, there is surprisingly little work that delivers implementable prescriptions for which set of items should be sponsored.444An interesting study of Farronato, Fradkin, and MacKay (2023) finds that Amazon favors its own brands in search. We study the problem of optimal advertisement design within the LMA framework. We provide simple operational solutions to the advertisement-design problem under the assumptions of attention scarcity (probability of following the advertisement decreases with the size of advertised set) and inverted-U attention (probability of following the advertisement first increases then decreases with the size of advertised set).

We show that the LMA model is characterized by two simple axioms. The first axiom is Block-IIA, which states that the relative choice frequency of alternative aa over bb is independent of the menu provided both aa and bb are advertised (or both not). The second axiom is Advertising Boost, which says that the relative choice frequency of an advertised alternative over an unadvertised one is weakly higher than when they are both not advertised. We then show that we can uniquely identify the Luce values and probability of following the advertisement from observed choice frequencies.

In addition to shifting attention, advertisements can also shape preferences. For instance, in our motivating example, if the advertised cars are SUVs, the consumer might perceive hatchbacks as less appealing. Indeed, a variety of studies show that, both experimentally and empirically, advertising plays dual roles in consumers’ decision making by affecting both the awareness of, and the preferences over, products (Barach, 1969; Gupta and Harris, 2010; Draganska and Klapper, 2011). We incorporate these dual roles of advertising by introducing A-LMA, which is a generalized version of LMA that allows the Luce value of an alternative to depend on the advertised set, so that the advertisement affects preferences through the Luce value.555It is termed the “representative utility” in Train (2009), which can also be interpreted as the average utility of an alternative among the population. We use “Luce value” and “utility” interchangeably throughout the paper. Given that the A-LMA is a more general version of the LMA, the axiom that characterizes A-LMA is weaker than Block-IIA. It states that the relative choice frequency of aa over bb is independent of the menu if both aa and bb are advertised (or not) given the same advertised set.

The Luce model is the nonparametric version of the multinomial logit model (McFadden, 1974), a workhorse of discrete choice modeling for advertising applications. In standard empirical settings, the two forces of advertising on preference and attention are difficult to disentangle because the same observed increase in choice probabilities for advertised products may reflect either greater attention or higher utility (or both). The key contribution of the A-LMA is to separate these two conceptually distinct channels from the choice data. We provide partial identification results of the advertisement-dependent Luce values and attention.666Partial identification is also obtained in the work on consideration set models in Barseghyan et al. (2021) and Lu (2022). Furthermore, we propose and characterize a parametric version of the A-LMA in which the model’s primitives are uniquely identified. We show that, under this specification, choice data can uniquely recover both the sign (positive or negative) and the magnitude of advertising’s effect on the utilities of both advertised and unadvertised alternatives, in addition to identifying the attention effect of advertising. Therefore, the novel take of this parametric version of the A-LMA is that it provides a tool to cleanly distinguish between the attention channel and preference channel.

Since advertised alternatives receive more attention than the unadvertised alternatives, LMA and A-LMA directly capture the “awareness” feature of advertising in Aaker and Myers (1982), Belch and Belch (1990), which declare that an important role of advertising is to remind consumers to consider the advertised products.777As discussed in Zeithammer and Lenk (2009), it is easier to make a choice when the consideration set is smaller. In the presence of advertising, the assumption that sometimes the individual only considers the intersection of the menu and the advertisement seems persuasive. Indeed, Mitra (1995), Shapiro, MacInnis, and Heckler (1997) find that a DM is more likely to consider those products that are advertised. Our assumption that the DM sometimes considers all the alternatives from the menu is consistent with a line of research showing that an individual constantly considers alternatives that are outside of the advertised set of products.888See, e.g., Goodman et al. (2013). Additionally, we assume that the probability of considering the advertised alternatives depends on both the advertisement and the menu. This is supported by experimental research on advertisements. For example, Goodman et al. (2013) find that the formation of consideration sets is affected by the menu size when two alternatives are labeled as “best seller”; Helmers, Krishnan and Patnam (2019) find that advertised products are more likely to be bought if the advertised set is smaller.

In the literature on stochastic consideration, most research, e.g., Manzini and Mariotti (2014), Brady and Rehbeck (2016), Aguiar, Boccardi and Kashaev (2023) assume that any subset of a given choice set can be a consideration set. A feature of the LMA and A-LMA is that, given a menu and an advertisement, there are only two possibilities for the consideration set, the entire menu or the set of available and advertised alternatives. We consider this simplification an advantage, as the computational burden when implementing our model in econometric analysis is substantially reduced, while it still captures the key idea of limited attention that an agent might only consider a subset of the choice set.999We discuss this computational issue in more detail in Section 7. This central mechanism, whereby advertising influences choice by probabilistically shifting attention to the advertised set, is also supported by empirical work in marketing. Zhang (2006) finds direct evidence that consumers sometimes consider only displays and featured advertisements, and sometimes evaluate the full set of alternatives.

Bagwell (2007) views advertising as persuasive, informative, and complementary. The persuasive view holds that advertising shifts preferences over alternatives directly. The informative view treats advertising as making options salient, expanding awareness, and guiding consumers to available alternatives. The complementary view posits that advertising enters utility directly as a consumption complement (e.g., status or reassurance). Our A-LMA captures these through two primitives: a consideration channel, which reflects the informative role of advertising by making advertised options more likely to be attended to, and an advertisement-dependent utility channel, which captures persuasive and complementary effects by allowing advertising to change the attractiveness of alternatives. In this way, our model’s testable restrictions and identification results enable empirical separation of the two channels without committing to a single view ex ante.

While advertising has been studied extensively in marketing, it has received relatively little attention in the literature on individual decision making. Cheung and Masatlioglu (2025a) make an important step in this direction by developing a recommendation framework that separates an attention channel from a utility channel. Our A-LMA differs in both channels: we impose a set-directed attention rule and allow advertisement-dependent Luce values without restricting utilities to two regimes.101010More specifically, Cheung and Masatlioglu (2025a) assume that the utility of an alternative aa is either u​(a)u\left(a\right) if aa is not recommended or u′​(a)u^{\prime}\left(a\right) if aa is recommended. Relatedly, Cheung and Masatlioglu (2025b) propose a Frame-Dependent Utility framework in which framed alternatives (e.g., recommended, featured, displayed) receive a utility premium. Recently, Li, Tang and Zhang (2025) develop an Association based Consideration rule, where they study how mental associations between alternatives influence decision-making.

The A-LMA is “preference-based”, as we assume that the utility of an alternative depends on the advertised set. This dependence relates our framework to a literature exploring reference-dependent preferences (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979; Kőszegi and Rabin, 2006; Kibris, Masatlioglu and Suleymanov, 2024).

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 lays out the stochastic choice environment with advertisement and introduces the LMA. In Section 3, we discuss the advertisement-design problem and derive implementable rules for optimal advertising. In Section 4, we provide an axiomatic characterization of the LMA, and establish point identification of the parameters. Next, we discuss empirical implications and connect the model to advertising regularities in Section 5. Section 6 generalizes the framework of LMA to A-LMA which allows advertisement-dependent utilities. We characterize the A-LMA and provide partial identification results. We also provide a parametric version of the A-LMA which identifies the attention and advertisement-dependent utilities uniquely. Section 7 compares our approach to the alternative models in the literature on advertising that emphasize only preference shifts, or fully flexible consideration. Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper.

2026-08-05.title: A unifying perspective on the collapse to the mean for law-invariant functionals
2026-08-05.abstract:
We revisit the “collapse to the mean” phenomenon, which refers to mild structural conditions, such as local linearity, that force a law-invariant functional φ\varphi defined on finite-mean random variables to depend solely on the expectation of its argument XX, and not on any other distributional feature.
Starting from a concise characterisation of the convex order, our simplified approach unifies and extends existing results without assuming the functional to be convex or monotone in the almost-sure order, and clarifies the conceptual foundations of the “collapse to the mean” phenomenon.
In addition, we establish a new “dual collapse” result for quasi-star-shaped functionals.
2026-08-05.introduction:
Defined on a domain 𝒳\mathcal{X} of random variables XX over a fixed probability space, law-invariant functionals assign values solely on the basis of the distribution of the argument XX in question.
Such functionals are widely used in economics, finance, and risk management to assess the utility, risk, or deviation from a benchmark of a random prospect.

The simplest examples of law-invariant functionals are expectation-based ones, where the assigned value is entirely determined by the mean of the argument (assuming such a mean exists).
Consequently, any two random variables with the same mean under the latent reference probability measure are mapped to the same value, irrespective of other distributional features in which they may differ, such as higher-order moments, symmetry, or tail behaviour.
By contrast, these features are often crucial for functionals assessing the riskiness of random prospects.
They directly impact the computation of classical risk metrics such as Value-at-Risk, Expected Shortfall and upper partial moments (McNeil et al., 2015, Chapter 2.3).
Insurance premia commonly add a deviation-measuring safety loading such as a fraction of variance or standard deviation to the actuarially fair price of a claim (Kaas et al., 2008, Chapter 5.3).
Moreover, since Markowitz (1952), it has been standard to select portfolios trading off the mean of random returns against their dispersion around the mean. Expectation-based functionals are therefore generally unsuited for risk management purposes.

In many contexts, however, such functionals are not pinned down in closed form directly but characterised by axioms, whose interplay and relation to other properties might not be transparent at first sight.
In this situation, the term “collapse to the mean” summarises at times surprising and seemingly unrelated conditions under which a law-invariant functional is necessarily—and potentially unintentionally—expectation-based.
Following the discussion in Bellini et al. (2021b), this is precisely the context of
Castagnoli et al. (2004) and Frittelli and Rosazza Gianin (2005), the earliest contributions on the collapse to the mean.
These challenge Wang (2000, 2002)’s harmonisation of financial and insurance pricing, which builds on Wang et al. (1997)’s axiomatisation of insurance pricing rules as law-invariant Choquet integrals.
They effectively question whether a pricing functional can sensibly be law invariant
by exposing the fundamental tension between the law invariance of a sublinear or convex pricing rule and the presence of nontrivial frictionlessly priced payoffs.
The only admissible pricing rule able to cope with both requirements is the expectation, the actuarially fair price, yet it does not contain any safety loading.

In other words, counter to the modeller’s intuition, a functional derived from seemingly reasonable axioms may discard all distributional information beyond the mean of its argument.
The repercussions of this phenomenon are not limited to insurance pricing; for example, (Bellini et al., 2021b, Section 5) interpret this result as the underpinning of the partial law invariance encountered in market-consistent valuation and apply it to capital requirements based on eligible assets in the spirit of Artzner et al. (2009).
In Liebrich and Svindland (2019) and Liebrich (2024), collapse-to-the-mean results (implicitly) serve as important tools in solving optimal risk sharing problems involving eligible assets or consistent risk measures.
A further example is Centrone and Rosazza Gianin (2025) in the context of capital allocation.

A growing body of literature has subsequently shown how robust the collapse-to-the-mean phenomenon is, and has streamlined and generalised the associated mathematical results.
While Amarante (2021) casts them in terms of the bipolar theorem, Bellini et al. (2021b), Chen et al. (2021), Liebrich and Munari (2022) and Amarante et al. (2024) have extended the analysis to more general spaces and classes of functionals; relaxed countable additivity of the reference measure; or replaced local linearity with conditions requiring, e.g., that risk is not increased when suitable prospects are added to the initial position.
These extensions broaden the economic implications of the phenomenon and reveal further limits to meaningful risk management wherever law invariance is imposed.

Beyond these contributions dedicated specifically to the collapse to the mean, the debate connects to further strands of the risk management literature.
A collapse to the mean can be interpreted as a failure of the “sensitivity to large losses” property of Herdegen et al. (2024). The conditions forcing expectation-basedness can be viewed through the lens of risk reducers, as studied for the convex order by Cheung et al. (2014), He et al. (2016) and for the Expected Shortfall by Herdegen et al. (2025).
Moreover, expectation-basedness coincides with the “risk neutrality” of Maccheroni et al. (2025), whose global properties of dependence neutrality and neutrality to full insurance are equivalent to the local conditions appearing in collapse-to-the-mean results.

A study closely related to the present paper is Liebrich and Munari (2022).
That work treats the collapse to the mean in as general a framework as possible and avoids assumptions of convexity or monotonicity in the almost-sure order where possible.
However, it does not provide a unified mathematical exposition with a single main result from which the individual case studies follow as corollaries.
As a consequence, its findings may appear fragmented or technical.

In the present paper, we address this limitation and contribute to the literature as follows.
First, we unify the bulk of existing results without imposing convexity or monotonicity assumptions.
Second, we derive the collapse-to-the-mean results not from law invariance per se, but from consistency with the convex order. Its concise characterisation in Shaked and Shanthikumar (2007) serves as a simple and transparent mathematical foundation, allowing to avoid dual methods and streamline proofs.
Third, this simplified perspective naturally leads to a generalisation of the existing results that covers the quasi-star-shaped functionals recently introduced by Han et al. (2025) and even potentially incomplete law-invariant preferences.
Fourth, we draw explicit connections between the collapse to the mean
and risk reducers, sensitivity to large losses, and insurance propensity, thereby involving a body of literature outside of the scope of preceding contributions and improving the relevance for risk management in actuarial and financial contexts.

The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 recalls the preliminaries, reviews the relevant existing results unified by the present approach, and discusses the connection between the collapse to the mean and recent contributions in the risk management literature. Section 3 presents and thoroughly discusses our main unifying results. The mathematical analysis and proofs of the main results are provided in Section 4.

2026-08-05.title: Does the Gender Wage Gap Originate at Labor Market Entry? Evidence from South Korea
2026-08-05.abstract: When in the lifecycle does a large gender wage gap emerge? South Korea has the largest gender pay gap in the OECD, 29%. Among recent college graduates the conditional gap is only 4.3% over 2008–2019, falling from 5.0% to 3.0%, and correcting for differential selection into full-time wage employment with semiparametric, machine-learning, and bounds methods leaves it unchanged. Among observed workers what remains sits at the top of the distribution. In Korean panel data the corrected gap widens severalfold across the prime-age workforce, where the selection correction becomes first order. Korea’s gender disparity is mostly generated after entry.
2026-08-05.introduction:
When in the lifecycle does the gender wage gap emerge? The answer matters for both economic understanding and policy design, yet it is difficult to establish because aggregate wage gaps conflate initial differentials with the cumulative effects of career interruptions, promotion differentials, occupational resorting, child penalties, and generational differences. This paper uses South Korea as a hard test of whether large gender gaps originate at labor market entry. [OECD (2024)] reports a gender pay gap of 29.3% for full-time Korean workers in 2023, about 2.6 times the OECD average of 11.3%, and [OECD (2026)] identifies it as the widest in the organisation. Korea also features institutional conditions that might generate both a large entry-level gap and employment selection: strong gender norms, a substantial gender employment gap, and sharp occupational segregation. If large entry-level gaps and substantial selection bias were to show up anywhere, this economy is a plausible place to expect them. Conversely, if entry-level selection bias proves negligible even in this hard-case setting, that would suggest it is less consequential in economies with smaller aggregate gaps and higher female participation.

This paper’s central message is that Korea’s large aggregate gap does not originate from labor market entry. Using the Graduates Occupational Mobility Survey (GOMS) data, I establish four findings that build to this conclusion. First, large national gender gaps can coexist with small conditional entry-level gaps. Among recent college graduates, the raw entry-level wage gap remains sizable (around 12%), but after controlling for educational background, age, and job characteristics, the conditional hourly wage gap is only 4.3% over 2008–2019 and it declines from 5.0% in 2008–2011 to 3.0% in 2016–2019. Second, this conclusion survives alternative flexible selection corrections that do not rely on exclusion restrictions, all of which yield estimates within half a log point of OLS. Third, the remaining entry-level gap is concentrated at the top of the wage distribution. Quantile regression estimates show a pronounced pattern by 2016–2019: the gap has effectively closed at the 10th percentile but remains approximately 5% at the 90th, consistent with [Goldin (2014)]’s hypothesis about high-paying positions (“greedy jobs”). Fourth, because the aggregate national gender gap combines within-cohort lifecycle divergence with differences across cohorts, the contrast between the small entry-level conditional gap and Korea’s large aggregate gap suggests that gender wage inequality is generated largely after entry.111For instance, [Kleven, Landais, and Leite-Mariante (2025)] estimate a child penalty in employment of 49% for South Korea, one of the largest among advanced economies. In their framework, the child penalty measures the post-childbirth divergence in employment between women and men.

To examine this lifecycle interpretation, I apply the same estimation battery to the Korean Labor and Income Panel Study (KLIPS) and trace the cross-sectional age profile of the gap across the prime-age workforce. The selection-corrected gap roughly doubles among college-educated workers, from about 8% at ages 24 to 35 to 17% at ages 24 to 55, and roughly triples across all workers, from about 7% to 21%. The selection correction, negligible at entry, becomes a first-order adjustment once the female employment “M-curve” takes hold.222The “M-curve” refers to the characteristic age profile of female labor force participation in Korea (and historically Japan): participation rises in the early career, falls during the prime marriage and childrearing years, and recovers later, tracing an “M” when plotted against age. Male participation, by contrast, is single-peaked. The entry-level gap is thus the low point of a lifecycle profile along which both the gap and the selection bias grow with age.

The methodological challenge in establishing these findings is that wages are observed only for the employed: if the unobservable determinants of employment correlate with wages, OLS estimates conditional on employment are biased, and the direction of that bias is what differential selection would reveal. This selection problem is a central econometric concern in the gender wage gap literature (Mulligan and Rubinstein, 2008; Blau et al., 2024). Because the missing wage offers cannot be recovered even by experimental variation, the sample selection framework is the natural econometric approach in this setting. The classical Heckman selection model (Heckman, 1979) imposes joint normality and its numerical properties can be poor without exclusion restrictions.333See the related discussions in Hay and Olsen (1984), Duan et al. (1984), Manning, Duan, and Rogers (1987), and Leung and Yu (1996). I therefore estimate the entry-level gap using the semiparametric selection model of Kim and Lee (2026), which achieves point identification without exclusion restrictions by exploiting nonlinearity in the selection process, a particular advantage here because credible variables that shift graduate employment without also shifting offered wages are difficult to defend. I then compare the results to debiased machine learning methods (Chernozhukov et al., 2018; Pan and Zhang, 2024) and to bounds approaches (Lee, 2009; Honoré and Hu, 2020).

The paper relates to three literatures. The first is the empirical literature on the gender wage gap and labor-force selection. The standard empirical starting point is to estimate wage gaps conditional on observables and decompose them using the Oaxaca-Blinder framework (Oaxaca, 1973; Blinder, 1973). Because these decompositions condition on observed employment, changing selection into work can distort both the level and the trend of measured gaps (Fortin, Lemieux, and Firpo, 2011). In the US literature, Blau and Kahn (2017) review the broad evidence on long-run gender wage convergence, while Goldin (2014) emphasize the role of temporal inflexibility in the remaining gap. On selection, Mulligan and Rubinstein (2008) attribute most of the measured narrowing to changes in female workforce composition. More recently, Blau et al. (2024) use the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) to expand wage coverage, compare several correction methods, and show that selection-corrected wage offers still converged substantially. Their preferred correction method relies on longitudinal wage histories and imputation to recover missing wage offers. This paper’s empirical design removes that data requirement: the semiparametric selection model is implemented directly on repeated cross-sections, without longitudinal wage information, which is what makes a selection-corrected estimate feasible for a nationally representative cohort observed once, at labor market entry, the career stage where no wage history yet exists.

The second is the econometric literature on sample selection. Semiparametric and nonparametric extensions of Heckman’s model relax its distributional assumption but typically still require exclusion restrictions for identification (Ahn and Powell, 1993; Das, Newey, and Vella, 2003; Newey, 2009; Machado, 2017); Chamberlain (1986) characterizes what identification requires without them. Bounding methods (Blundell et al., 2007; Lee, 2009; Honoré and Hu, 2020) weaken these requirements, but at the cost of relying on special support conditions or partial identification. More recently, Kim and Lee (2026) show that point identification can be achieved without exclusion restrictions when the selection process is sufficiently nonlinear, and propose a semiparametric two-step sieve plug-in estimator. Pan and Zhang (2024) develop a complementary debiased machine learning approach. I use these recent methods together with Lee and Honoré-Hu bounds to ask whether the paper’s headline finding is robust to different identifying assumptions about selection.

The third is the entry-level gender gap literature. Studies that follow a cohort over time find a small gap at entry that widens sharply thereafter. Among US elite professionals like MBAs and lawyers, females and males start at near-identical earnings yet diverge over their careers.444Female and male MBAs open an almost 60 log point male advantage within a decade (Bertrand, Goldin, and Katz, 2010), and among lawyers early gaps are modest relative to the much larger gaps that emerge later (Wood, Corcoran, and Courant, 1993; Noonan, Corcoran, and Courant, 2005), with the divergence traced to billable hours and client revenue (Azmat and Ferrer, 2017). The pattern is not confined to elites: for US college graduates the gap expands by about 34 log points over the early career (Goldin et al., 2017).555This estimated gap is split roughly evenly between sorting into higher-paying positions, industries, and firms (about 44%) and within-firm advancement (about 56%). Manning and Swaffield (2008) also show that the gap is near zero among UK labor-market entrants of all education levels and reaches roughly 25 log points after ten years. By contrast, studies measuring the gap among recent graduates often find it nontrivial already at job entry.666A gap of 10–15% survives controls for major, GPA, and institution among US college graduates (Weinberger, 1998), and up to three-quarters of the entry gap remains unexplained (Joy, 2003); among recent German graduates the raw gap is 20 log points, narrowing to 5–10 after extensive controls (Francesconi and Parey, 2018), and 12.5 log points, narrowing to 4.7 with occupation controls (Sandner and Yükselen, 2025); recent Italian graduates show a 5.6% hourly gap whose unexplained component rises across the wage distribution (Piazzalunga, 2018); and whole-population Russian register data document a 14% raw entry gap that widens to about 26% more than four years after graduation (Rozhkova, Roshchin, and Yemelina, 2024). Across college-educated workers more broadly, college major and occupational sorting account for a substantial share of the gender gap (Black et al., 2008; Sloane, Hurst, and Black, 2021). Almost all of this evidence conditions on the employed sample without formal selection correction. Relative to this literature, I contribute a nationally representative, all-field entry cohort in which selection into employment is not assumed away but corrected and tested directly, and I then place the entry estimate in lifecycle context with the same methods: a small declining conditional gap alongside a sizable raw gap mostly generated after labor market entry.777Prior studies show that Korea’s aggregate gender wage gap widens sharply over the lifecycle (Dynan, Kirkegaard, and Stansbury, 2022; Stansbury, Kirkegaard, and Dynan, 2024) and that it narrowed across the wage distribution between 2003 and 2016 (Tromp, 2019). Conditions at entry also have lasting and gender-asymmetric consequences: graduating into the Asian financial crisis produced persistent employment and earnings losses for Korean men but raised childbearing among women (Choi et al., 2020), and exposure to that recession altered field of study and the quality of first jobs (Choi et al., 2025). Among studies on recent graduates, Tromp and Kwak (2022) report a raw entry-level gap of 0.190 log points, at least half the aggregate gap, Cho (2024) documents substantial narrowing by 2019, Kim and Oh (2022) link the graduate gap to regional variation in gender prejudice, and Kim and Shin (2024) emphasize gender differences in earnings growth after the school-to-work transition. Yet these papers largely condition on the employed sample and therefore do not establish whether differential employment selection materially biases entry-level estimates. Formal selection correction in the Korean literature remains rare, with Cho and Ko (2023) and Moon and Kim (2023) applying Heckman models and Tromp and Richey (2026) using imputation methods. This paper extends that literature by providing extensive evidence on the corrected entry-level gap.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 presents the econometric framework. Section 3 describes the data. Section 4 reports the main results and robustness analyses. Section 5 estimates the lifecycle evolution of the gender wage gap using Korean panel data. Section 6 concludes.

2026-08-05.title: Mandate without Managers: Automated Market Makers as Verifiable Portfolio Products
2026-08-05.subjects: Trading and Market Microstructure (q-fin.TR); Mathematical Finance (q-fin.MF); Portfolio Management (q-fin.PM)
2026-08-05.abstract: Automated market makers (AMMs) are typically interpreted and evaluated as decentralized exchanges. Herein, we take the perspective envisioned by Balancer that an AMM can also be viewed as a portfolio technology that programmatically enforces an economic mandate. In particular, we follow the geometric mean market maker (G3M) invariant employed by that protocol in order to enforce a target-weighted portfolio. We introduce a multi-asset fee structure to the G3M under which competitive arbitrage implements a band-rebalancing strategy with mis-weighting bounded ex ante, allowing compliance with the mandate to be verified directly from the pool’s observable holdings. We then compare simulated G3M portfolios against the realized performance of VBIAX, EQL, and EDOW on annualized returns and tracking error against the portfolio mandate. Across these historical case studies, and using arbitrage-only order flow, the G3M is found to outperform the incumbent funds in both metrics for certain fee ranges.
2026-08-05.introduction:
Target-weight portfolio mandates are among the most common products in traditional asset management. Financial advisors routinely recommend allocations such as 60% equity and 40% fixed income. Certain such positions are so common that they are offered as mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs). For these funds, the product is both the asset holdings and the value of the commitment to maintain the stated allocation over time. Unlike the better known market cap weighted ETFs, these target weighted ETFs require active rebalancing which can be costly to achieve [4].

By following a mathematical invariant, an automated market maker (AMM) offers a programmatic way to implement such a commitment. Though an AMM is typically interpreted as a rule governing the terms at which assets can be exchanged [1, 2], the same automation also determines the composition of the reserves held on behalf of liquidity providers (LPs). In this sense, an AMM is simultaneously an exchange and a portfolio rule. From the portfolio perspective, the role of the arbitrageur changes to that of an external rebalancing agent who is compensated by the arbitrage profits extracted from the LPs. The AMM pool, therefore, maintains its mandate algorithmically and without managerial discretion.
The portfolio interpretation of an AMM is particularly direct for the geometric mean market maker (G3M) as this AMM encodes a target-weighted portfolio [5, 6]. This viewpoint has been commercialized by Balancer [7] and QuantAMM [10, 12] for crypto-assets.

We explore the G3M as a portfolio rebalancing technology both theoretically and empirically.
Section 2 provides background on the G3M and introduces a novel fee structure under which competitive arbitrage constrains the realized portfolio weights to an explicitly characterized neighborhood of the target weights. This permits the fee-bearing G3M to be interpreted as a band-rebalanced target-weight strategy. This extends the two-asset setting of [6] (under a modified fee structure) to provide a closed-form characterization of the fee-induced no-arbitrage region in weight space for a multi-asset G3M.
Section 3 compares simulated G3M portfolios with real funds to empirically assess whether AMMs can serve as a practical portfolio technology when competing against incumbent funds. This builds upon the work of [11] to consider more realistic benchmarks against which to evaluate AMM performance. As far as we are aware, we provide the first direct comparison between an AMM-held portfolio and traditional mutual funds and ETFs.
Across three case studies, we find that the G3M, in certain parameter ranges under purely adversarial order flow, can dominate the incumbent fund in both returns and tracking error against the economic mandate.

2026-08-05.title: Preference robust distortion risk measures
2026-08-05.subjects: Risk Management (q-fin.RM); General Economics (econ.GN); Theoretical Economics (econ.TH); Mathematical Finance (q-fin.MF)
2026-08-05.introduction:
In decision-making under uncertainty, particularly in finance, insurance, and risk management, a decision maker must evaluate and rank random outcomes. A common approach is to assess an outcome’s risk profile using a risk measure, such as Value-at-Risk, Tail Value-at-Risk, and Wang transform, that are special cases of generalised distortion risk measures (signed Choquet integral). A distortion risk measure evaluates the risk of a position using a distortion (or weight function), which reflects the decision maker’s risk preferences. The shape of this distortion captures phenomena like loss aversion or over/under-weighting of tail probabilities (Dhaene et al. 2012, Prelec 1998, Wang et al. 2020).

Classical robustness frameworks in stochastic optimization primarily address distributional ambiguity, which refers to uncertainty in the probability distribution of the underlying risk factors, while the risk functional itself remains fixed (Blanchet and Murthy 2019, Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn 2018); recent work optimises distortion riskmetrics (Pesenti et al. 2025) and distorted expectations (Cai et al. 2025) over a set of plausible distributions, again holding the distortion — and hence the risk preference — fixed. In many real-world contexts, however, the decision maker’s preferences, i.e., in our setting, the distortion function, may also be ambiguous. This ambiguity can arise from estimation errors in eliciting preferences, as preferences are typically not fully known in practice. This gives rise to the concept of preference robustness, where decisions must be robust to ambiguity in the risk functional itself, a perspective that has recently gained interest, in particular in the context of ambiguity on the utility or loss function, see e.g., Armbruster and Delage (2015), Haskell et al. (2022), Delage et al. (2022), Guo et al. (2024), Hu et al. (2025), Liu et al. (2025), Zhang et al. (2025). For eliciting preference in a real-data study we refer to Bianchi and Tallon (2019), who consider the connection between portfolio choices and ambiguity preferences, and to Cavatorta and Schröder (2019) who develop a survey for eliciting preferences. The elicitation of utility and probability weighting functions under rank-dependent and prospect-theoretic models is well studied in the decision-theoretic literature (Wakker and Deneffe 1996, Abdellaoui 2000, Bleichrodt and Pinto 2000). Works related to preference robust risk measures include Guo and Xu (2022) who consider moment-type ambiguity sets that encompass lotteries and pairwise comparisons, and Wang and Xu (2023) who derive a numerical approach (linear program) for discrete loss distribution. Liu (2024) consider ambiguity sets for distortion risk measures characterised by lotteries, and in the context of optimal insurance demand, Boonen and Jiang (2025) consider preference robustness with continuous loss distribution with ambiguity characterised by lotteries for which the worst-case distortion function is reduced to a piecewise linear function, making the problem tractable via linear programming.

In this paper, we develop a comprehensive framework for preference-robust decision making when preferences are modelled via generalised distortion risk measures or using rank-dependent utility (RDU). Unlike works that construct ambiguity sets from pairwise lottery comparisons (Delage and Li 2018, Guo and Xu 2022, Liu et al. 2025), we choose a reference distortion function (the decision maker’s “best guess”) and consider all plausible distortions within a neighbourhood defined by a statistical divergence. Specifically, we construct ambiguity sets using the Wasserstein distance and the more flexible class of Bregman divergences. This approach provides a natural, geometric way to quantify deviations from a reference preference and allows for asymmetric treatments of deviations. While the Wasserstein distance is popular for modelling (distributional) uncertainty, the Bregman-Wasserstein divergences has only recently been used for quantifying ambiguity, see e.g., Guo et al. (2017), Tam and Pesenti (2025) and Pesenti et al. (2024), Pesenti and Nguyen (2026) in a portfolio choice context.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we develop a framework for ambiguity in
the risk functional itself: instead of perturbing the loss distribution
(distributional robustness), we place
a neighbourhood around a reference distortion (weight) function, built either from
the Wasserstein distance or from a family of asymmetric Bregman divergences that
can weight deviations on the left and right tails differently. When the ambiguity set is constructed via the Wasserstein distance, the results reveal a simple, additive structure: the robust risk measure equals the original risk measure plus (or minus) a penalty proportional to the second moment of the risk exposure. In other words, preference ambiguity endogenously generates a second moment loading. Second, we derive closed-form best- and worst-case
generalised distortion risk measures under economically meaningful
restrictions of the ambiguity set, e.g., coherent distortion risk measures and elicited pairwise preferences between
lotteries. We furthermore characterise the smallest radius εmin{\varepsilon}_{\min} consistent with a
set of revealed preferences, suggesting a natural choice of the
ambiguity radius. Third, we show that robustifying expected utility over such ambiguity
neighbourhoods yield a rank-dependent utility with an explicitly computable
distortion; this accommodates the Allais paradox and inverse-S probability
weighting, and we illustrate it on a portfolio comparison in which mean–variance
and Expected Shortfall (ES) rank two financial positions in opposite orders.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 formally introduces the setting of preference robustness for generalised distortion risk measures, defines the ambiguity sets using the Wasserstein distance and the Bregman divergence, and discusses choices of Bregman generators. Section 3 presents our main theoretical results (the preference robust distortion risk measure under Bregman uncertainty) and extends the results to include constraints such that the robust preference is coherent or consistent with lotteries. Section 4 applies our framework to RDU, which can be viewed as preference robust expected utility. We demonstrate how RDU naturally arises as a preference robust expected utility that satisfies the Allais paradox or allows for Inverse-S shape preferences. We conclude in Section 5 and delegated all proofs to Section 6.

2026-08-05.title: Reviving Micro Real Rigidities: The Importance of Demand Shocks
2026-08-05.authors: S. Borağan Aruoba,Eugene Oue,Felipe Saffie,Jonathan L. Willis
2026-08-05.abstract: We revisit micro real rigidities as a source of monetary non-neutrality in a menu-cost model with variable markups, using firm-level evidence to pin down key primitives. We embed a non-CES demand system in a quantitative monetary model and use firm-dynamics evidence to identify demand curvature and firm-level productivity and demand processes. The calibrated model matches untargeted micro pricing moments, the markup distribution, and cost pass-through, while generating comparable non-neutrality. The key innovation is an empirically supported placement of idiosyncratic demand shocks that shifts residual demand, thereby moving desired markups and prices under non-CES demand. The broader implication is that this calibrated model provides a portable framework linking monetary economics with trade and IO evidence.
2026-08-05.introduction:
Modeling the response of output and prices to monetary policy shocks has long been central to macroeconomic research. Empirical studies consistently show that such shocks have persistent and substantial effects on real output (christiano1999monetary; ramey2016macroeconomic). These real effects arise because prices do not fully adjust to nominal disturbances. How much they adjust depends on two distinct forces: nominal frictions that prevent firms from changing prices, and structural features of demand and costs that limit how much firms want to adjust prices even when they can. ball1990real show that nominal frictions alone are insufficient, and that a second force, which they termed real rigidities, is necessary to generate quantitatively significant monetary non-neutrality.111The term real rigidities is standard in the macroeconomic literature following ball1990real. Closely related mechanisms, however, are widely studied in the industrial organization and international trade literatures under different terminologies, including incomplete cost pass-through, variable markups, demand curvature, and strategic complementarities in pricing. Thus, what macroeconomists refer to as real rigidities largely corresponds to features of demand systems, competitive structure, and markup adjustment that are central objects of study in these other fields.

A key determinant of how much firms want to adjust prices is the shape of the demand they face. Under constant elasticity of substitution (CES) demand, the standard assumption in quantitative pricing models, desired markups are constant and firms pass cost changes to prices one for one. Deviations from CES, where demand becomes more or less price sensitive depending on a firm’s market share, generate variable markups and incomplete pass-through of cost shocks, features that are quantitatively important across many fields of economics. Non-CES demand systems such as kimball1995quantitative are widely used to study markup variability (edmond2018costly; arkolakis2019elusive), exchange rate pass-through (gopinath2010frequency; gopinath2011search; amiti2019international; berger2019shocks), and inflation dynamics (smets2007shocks; harding2022resolving; harding2023understanding; fujiwara2022competition). Yet in the quantitative monetary economics literature, their adoption has been limited.

Instead, the quantitative monetary economics literature has primarily relied on macro-level real rigidities to amplify the real effects of nominal shocks, including production networks with sticky intermediate inputs (basu1995intermediate; nakamura2010monetary), segmented labor markets (woodford2003; gertler2008phillips), and real wage rigidity (blanchard2007real). These mechanisms are effective at generating monetary non-neutrality, but they operate at the aggregate level and bypass the firm-level demand structure that governs pricing, markups, and pass-through. As a result, a natural connection between the monetary pricing literature and a large body of work in industrial organization, trade, and firm dynamics, where the shape of demand and its interaction with firm-level shocks are central objects of study, has remained largely detached.

This paper bridges this gap by bringing an empirically disciplined non-CES demand system into a quantitative monetary economics model. We make three contributions. First, we show theoretically how variable markups interact with idiosyncratic demand shocks to shape firms’ desired prices, and we identify firm-level moments that discipline the key demand parameters. Second, we build a menu-cost model calibrated to firm-level evidence on productivity and demand processes from foster2008reallocation, leaving standard pricing moments untargeted, and show that the model matches them well alongside the markup distribution, cost pass-through rates, and firm growth dynamics. Third, we show that the estimated demand system generates monetary non-neutrality comparable in magnitude to the macro-level mechanisms that the literature has pursued. The key innovation is to discipline and incorporate idiosyncratic demand shocks, which under non-CES demand move desired markups and prices.

The theoretical contribution, developed in Section 2, can be summarized as follows. Under CES demand, the elasticity a firm faces is constant, so the markup over marginal cost is constant, and only shocks to marginal cost, such as productivity shocks, pass through to prices. In this case, prices and productivity are perfectly negatively correlated, leading to a full pass-through of cost shocks to prices. However, a large body of empirical work in trade, industrial organization, and macroeconomics documents that the pass-through of cost shocks to prices is well below one, typically in the range of 20 to 50 percent. This is evidence that demand elasticities, or equivalently markups, are not constant, which is precisely what non-CES demand systems deliver. Under the standard parametrization of kimball1995quantitative, for instance, a firm with a larger effective market share faces less price-sensitive demand, allowing it to charge a higher markup.

This variable-elasticity structure has two implications. First, it generates incomplete pass-through of cost shocks, as changes in output move the firm along its demand curve and partially offset the incentive to adjust prices. Second, it opens the door for demand shocks to affect desired prices: a positive demand shock that raises a firm’s effective market share shifts the residual demand conditions it faces and raises its desired markup and its desired price. The price-productivity correlation estimated at −0.54-0.54 by foster2008reallocation, far from the −1-1 implied by CES, is direct evidence that demand shocks move desired markups in the data. Moreover, the distance from −1-1 and the estimate of the demand elasticity from the same study provide a strategy to identify the shape of the demand system.

We implement this identification strategy in a menu-cost model with a kimball1995quantitative demand system, calibrated to match firm-level moments from foster2008reallocation. This study is among the few that separately identify productivity and demand processes at the firm level using data on prices, quantities, and inputs for U.S. manufacturing firms. We target the persistence and cross-sectional dispersion of firm-level productivity and demand, the price-productivity correlation, an estimate of the demand elasticity, and the frequency of price changes. Importantly, we do not target any other pricing moments. Despite this, the calibrated model replicates the average size and direction of price changes, the dispersion of non-zero price adjustments, and a mildly downward-sloping hazard of price adjustment, all consistent with U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) microdata. The model also generates a cross-sectional distribution of markups that closely resembles estimates from Compustat data, and a cost pass-through rate of 43 percent, within the range documented in the empirical literature.222aruoba2025pricing underscore the flexibility of the Kimball framework using Chilean microdata, incorporating additional features such as leptokurtic shocks and news shocks. While distinct from our approach, their findings further highlight the value of this framework for explaining pricing behavior. These results show that a model disciplined by firm dynamics evidence can account for pricing patterns that the literature has traditionally targeted directly.

We assess the robustness of these results along several dimensions. We recalibrate the model using firm-level estimates from Colombian manufacturing data from eslava2024size, who employ an alternative methodology that relaxes the orthogonality assumption between productivity and demand shocks. The qualitative patterns are similar. We also show that the results are stable when we allow correlated shocks, target a broader set of moments, or introduce leptokurtic demand shocks to match the kurtosis of price changes.

Turning to monetary non-neutrality, the calibrated model generates cumulative output responses to a nominal expenditure shock approximately 34% larger than that produced by a comparable CES model. Two forces drive this result: the non-CES demand system, which induces strategic complementarity in pricing, and the inclusion of both productivity and demand shocks, which weakens selection with respect to the aggregate shock by increasing the share of adjusters responding to idiosyncratic conditions rather than the aggregate disturbance. The first force accounts for the larger share of the amplification. Notably, our micro-calibrated demand system more than doubles monetary non-neutrality even in a calvo1983staggered model, where selection is absent by construction. The degree of non-neutrality generated by our model is comparable to that reported in frameworks relying on macro-level complementarities, such as the multi-sector production network model of nakamura2010monetary.

Our paper contributes to the quantitative menu cost literature initiated by golosov2007menu, who show that standard menu-cost models with CES demand generate limited monetary non-neutrality. A key reason non-CES demand was set aside in this literature is the finding by klenow2016real that, in productivity-only calibrations with variable markups, matching the distribution of price changes requires very volatile idiosyncratic driving forces, with counterfactual implications for observable firm-level outcomes. We show that this tension is conditional on two features of their analysis: the absence of idiosyncratic demand shocks, and the treatment of demand curvature as given rather than estimated from firm-level data. In Section 5, we restate the analysis in terms of observable moments and show that, once curvature is disciplined and demand shocks are included, the tension disappears.

Our work is complementary to mongey2021market, who shows that strategic interactions in a dynamic oligopoly model can also overturn the klenow2016real finding. However, here our approach is different: rather than proposing a different market structure, we aim to make the benchmark framework of monopolistic competition with non-CES demand, one commonly used elsewhere in economics, empirically disciplined and quantitatively usable in the monetary economics literature. In fact, wang2022dynamic provide a bridge between these approaches by showing that, for standard monetary experiments, an oligopolistic model can be well approximated by a non-strategic benchmark with modified Kimball preferences, with most quantitative effects operating through residual-demand feedback rather than strategic interaction. This supports the use of a disciplined Kimball demand system as a parsimonious and portable reduced form across applications. beck2020price provide micro-based estimates of demand elasticities and super-elasticities using European data, finding moderate curvature that on its own generates limited non-neutrality, which underscores the importance of incorporating demand shocks as we do. More broadly, our identification strategy is part of a growing effort to discipline pricing primitives using firm-level microdata rather than aggregate moments, as in gagliardone2025anatomy.

Firms may also find relative price adjustments costly if they face increasing marginal costs. When marginal costs rise with output, per-unit profits fall as firms expand, restraining price cuts and generating strategic complementarity through the cost side. Cost-side mechanisms include decreasing returns to scale (burstein2007prices) and segmented input markets (woodford2003; gertler2008phillips). We explore this alternative in Section 5 and find that it can match several moments of the data, but requires very low returns to scale and does not replicate the empirical markup distribution as well as the demand-side specification.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 develops a simple theoretical framework that formalizes the role of demand curvature and idiosyncratic demand shocks in price setting, and establishes the identification results summarized above. Section 3 introduces the quantitative menu-cost model. Section 4 describes the calibration strategy and reports the fit to targeted and untargeted moments. Section 5 discusses external validity and presents robustness exercises, including the Klenow–Willis variants and the cost-side alternative. Section 6 examines the implications for monetary non-neutrality. Section 7 concludes.

2026-08-05.title: Raising Rivals' Costs on Hybrid Platforms: The Complementarity of Fees and Self-Preferencing
2026-08-05.abstract: Hybrid platforms disadvantage third-party sellers through the platform fee and self-preferencing, and regulators have worried that constraining either instrument may intensify the other. We model a platform that chooses both instruments and find the opposite: single-instrument regulation is effective because the instruments are strategic complements, and regulating either instrument curbs the other. We also find that the two instruments achieve what monopolization achieves, higher prices and reduced consumer welfare, while passing every conventional antitrust test.
2026-08-05.introduction:
A growing share of online retail flows through hybrid platforms: marketplaces that host independent third-party sellers and sell their own first-party products alongside them. Amazon is the largest example, but the same structure characterizes Coupang in South Korea, JD.com in China, Walmart Marketplace and Target Plus in the United States, Otto in Germany, Flipkart in India, and Rakuten in Japan. In each case, the platform sets the rules of the marketplace it competes in. It chooses the fee paid by third-party sellers, the visibility its first-party products receive in search and recommendation, and the price of those products. These choices have drawn antitrust attention in the United States, the European Union, and several Asian countries.

The fee is the analytical core of the arrangement. It inflates third-party sellers’ effective marginal cost, contracts the third-party segment, and diverts demand toward the fee-exempt first-party product. This is exclusion by raising rivals’ costs in the sense of Salop and Scheffman (1983), with one consequential difference: the cost-raising instrument is not an expenditure the platform makes but revenue it collects. A classical cost-raiser excludes only when the outlay is worth it. Here the exclusion pays for itself.

We develop a tractable theoretical model of a hybrid platform and ask how its ad valorem fee τ\tau on third-party revenue, self-preferencing intensity σ\sigma, and first-party price pAp_{A} are jointly determined in equilibrium, and what the welfare and policy implications are. The model has a free-entry continuum of symmetric third-party sellers and a logit demand system. The first-party product is exempt from the fee, and self-preferencing enters the discrete-choice utility as a chosen boost to its visibility.

We make four contributions. First, fees and self-preferencing are strategic complements. The platform’s profit is supermodular in (τ,σ)(\tau,\sigma): a higher fee raises the marginal profitability of self-preferencing, and more self-preferencing raises the marginal profitability of the fee. This is the central finding. The welfare harm runs entirely through the fee. Under free entry, consumer welfare is pinned down by τ\tau alone, so self-preferencing has zero direct effect on consumers. The platform’s privately optimal fee strictly exceeds the welfare-maximizing level, with a computable deadweight loss.

Second, single-instrument regulation is effective. A common concern in platform regulation is that constraining one instrument simply shifts the platform’s effort to another. Strategic complementarity implies the opposite. A binding fee cap lowers the platform’s chosen self-preferencing, and a non-discrimination mandate that forces σ=0\sigma=0 lowers the platform’s chosen fee. The European Union’s Digital Markets Act self-preferencing prohibition can therefore be effective on its own, and adding a fee cap makes the combined regime weakly better than either instrument alone.

Third, the conduct achieves what monopolization achieves, higher prices and reduced consumer welfare, without its markers. The marketplace can therefore appear competitive to standard antitrust tests. Those tests look for sacrifice, for eliminated rivals, and for concentration. The platform’s exclusionary instrument is self-financing, so there is no sacrifice to detect. Free entry holds per-seller profit at zero, so rivals are displaced at break-even rather than eliminated. Concentration is uninformative about the harm. A higher fee does reduce the seller count, but two configurations with the same seller count, Herfindahl-Hirschman index, and per-seller profit can still differ in consumer welfare.

Fourth, we embed the static problem in two dynamic environments, one for each reading of observed platform behavior: aggregate expansion has looked broadly monotone, while individual products are launched and withdrawn continually. The first environment takes the aggregate view. When entry is irreversible and categories differ in size, the platform gradually expands the set of categories in which it sells its first-party product, its footprint hereafter. Each new category lets it extract additional rent from the rest, so the fee rises with the footprint and stabilizes once the expansion ends, a pattern we call the transitional ratchet. The second environment takes the product-level view: products turn over, so the active footprint can contract and the path need not be monotone. We characterize an exact period-three window in which footprint, fee, and welfare cycle indefinitely, and show that chaotic equilibrium paths exist. Both environments point the regulator toward the footprint rather than the fee path.

Our work belongs to a small but rapidly growing theoretical literature on hybrid platforms. Anderson and Bedre-Defolie (2024) prove that a vertically integrated platform sets a higher fee than a pure marketplace, and that the fee rises as the platform’s product range grows. Dendorfer (2024) decomposes the two sides of platform integration: first-party selling raises welfare by mitigating double marginalization, while self-preferencing erodes part of that gain, so welfare is highest when the platform does not self-prefer. Etro (2023) embeds free entry and finds that the welfare effect of private-label entry is conditional. Hagiu et al. (2022) analyze when platforms should be permitted to sell alongside merchants and show that narrow bans on imitation and self-preferencing can dominate a blanket prohibition on the dual mode. These papers analyze the platform’s instruments largely in isolation or in regime-comparison form, which leaves the sign of the interaction between them undetermined. Our contribution is to model (τ,σ)(\tau,\sigma) as joint continuous choices and sign their interaction, to derive the regulatory and doctrinal consequences of that sign, and to embed the static problem in dynamic environments that separate the footprint distortion from the fee distortion.

The model also relates to the wider raising-rivals’-costs and vertical-foreclosure literatures. Salop and Scheffman (1983) and Krattenmaker and Salop (1986) establish that a firm may spend to inflate rivals’ costs, a costly commitment to be recouped after exclusion. Our addition to this literature is the observation that the hybrid platform’s exclusion is self-financing, so there is no outlay to recover and the recoupment screen never applies. The vertical foreclosure tradition (Rey and Tirole, 2007; Ordover et al., 1990) examines how control of an essential input extends market power downstream, and Choné et al. (2024) show how integration eliminates double marginalization while biasing the make-or-buy decision against independent suppliers. Here the foreclosure operates through fees and visibility rather than denial of access. Our dynamic results connect to the literature on erratic equilibrium paths in optimizing economies (Benhabib and Day, 1982; Grandmont, 1985; Boldrin and Montrucchio, 1986), with one difference: there the optimizer chooses its next state directly, while here the footprint evolves through a fixed turnover technology that the platform’s instruments can only shift. The empirical literature (Farronato et al., 2023; Waldfogel, 2024; Hartzell and Haupt, 2025; Zhu and Liu, 2018) documents the patterns the model rationalizes.

2026-08-05.title: Measuring the engine of a liquidation cascade: subcritical branching inside a first-order transition
2026-08-05.comment: . Part II of a series; Part I isarXiv:2607.27070
2026-08-05.abstract:
We study seven major crypto-perpetual liquidation cascades (2022–2025), and in
the largest of them we can watch the mechanism directly. From the on-chain fill
log of a fully transparent venue we measure the branching ratio of that
event—the October 2025 crash, the largest on record—in flight, with
both of its factors observed and no free constants. It ran deeply subcritical: the structural ratio and the
amplification bookkeeping both place it at λ^≈0.1\hat{\lambda}\approx 0.1–0.20.2
throughout, and a third, flow-based estimator—whose calm-market level is
mechanically inflated and must be read as a trajectory—falls through the
climax rather than rising. All three agree on subcriticality within the venue,
not on a common numerical level. Alongside them, 88%88\% of all post-onset forced
selling landed within thirty minutes and 63%63\% of it was absorbed off-book by the
venue’s backstop, which drives the branching ratio down precisely at the
climax. Across the full set of seven, at onset—the minute ending the steepest
hour of each crash—the order parameter (mean inter-asset coupling) jumps by
between 1.61.6 and 4.44.4 baseline standard deviations into a near-fully-ordered
phase, while the susceptibility proxy χ=N​Var​(ci​j)\chi=N\,\mathrm{Var}(c_{ij})
collapses in five of the seven events and diverges in none; the jump is
invariant under subsampling (N=8N=8–2828). The transition is abrupt and
scale-robust rather than critical, and its in-cascade signature lives in the
liquidity
sector: price impact spikes on two venues and two instruments (a factor of
1.21.2–3.53.5 regressed, 3.23.2–9.19.1 quoted directly) while open interest clears
by 2525–70%70\%. The natural mechanistic account—a Galton–Watson cascade with
λ=k​ρ~\lambda=k\tilde{\rho} (impact per forced dollar ×\times forced notional per
unit relative move)—is then eliminated as a description of the
pre-cascade state: both of its falsifiable predictions fail at simulated
power ≥0.96\geq 0.96, on proxied and on directly measured regressors alike. Severity
is set by shock ×\times map-in-path ×\times liquidity withdrawal rather than by
a diverging multiplier, which is why none of the scalar pre-state measures we
can construct grades it.
2026-08-05.introduction:
Whether large market crashes are critical transitions—endogenous
instabilities that a system approaches gradually, shedding resilience until an
infinitesimal shock tips it over—is among the oldest questions in the physics
of markets. The program has a long lineage, from the log-periodic critical-point
picture of Johansen et al. (2000) and Sornette (2003) to its
operational arm, the theory of early-warning signals (EWS): near a critical point
the dominant relaxation mode slows, so fluctuations grow more autocorrelated and
more variable ahead of the transition (Scheffer et al., 2009). Part I of this
series (Garcia Seuma, 2026) put that operational claim to the test on seven major
BTC perpetual-futures liquidation cascades (2022–2025) and found it wanting: no
single-variable early-warning signal is event-invariant, and the failures are
structured—critical slowing down is absent precisely where the shock is most
abrupt, echoing earlier doubts that financial meltdowns are critical transitions
at all (Guttal et al., 2016).

A negative result on indicators poses, but cannot answer, the prior
question: what is the order of the transition? Criticality is a statement
about collective structure, not about any single series, and a first-order
transition can jump discontinuously with no variable slowing beforehand—exactly
the signature Part I reported. Order must therefore be measured where it lives, in
the market’s correlation fabric, rather than inferred from the memory of one
price. Section 3 does this directly.

A leveraged market makes a second, usually inaccessible, question answerable: the
mechanism. The feedback laws here are not hidden model assumptions but
published exchange rules—the liquidation engine, funding, and the backstop that
clears insolvent positions. The natural mechanistic account is a branching
cascade, in which each forced sale moves the price and triggers, on average, some
number of further liquidations (Thurner et al., 2012; Filimonov and Sornette, 2012; Cont and Wagalath, 2016).
On Hyperliquid, a fully on-chain venue, every open position and every forced fill
is public, so the offspring mean of that cascade—the branching ratio
λ\lambda—can be measured rather than fitted from aggregate reflexivity.
We do exactly that, for the October 2025 cascade—the largest single-day
liquidation event recorded in crypto-perpetual markets
(Marshall, 2025; Chitra, 2025)—and the answer is that it never came
near the critical boundary.

We make four contributions, listed here in reading order. (i) We characterize the
transition as first-order in its signatures: at onset the order parameter
jumps into a near-fully-ordered phase while the susceptibility proxy
collapses rather than diverges, and the jump is invariant under
subsampling—a control that rules out panel composition and small-panel
artefacts as its source (Sec. 3). (ii) We locate the in-cascade
signature in the liquidity sector: price impact spikes and open interest clears,
on two venues and two independent measurements of impact (Sec. 4).
(iii) We eliminate the branching model as an account of the pre-cascade
state: both of its falsifiable predictions fail with simulated power ≥0.96\geq 0.96,
on proxied and on directly measured regressors alike (Sec. 5).
(iv) And—the result that motivates the other three—we provide, to our
knowledge, the first in-flight measurement of a record cascade’s branching
ratio, from Hyperliquid’s fill log, with both factors observed and no free
constants: subcritical throughout, front-loaded almost to instantaneity, and with
most of the offspring absorbed off-book by the venue backstop, so that the
exchange’s own liquidation waterfall suppresses the very feedback the model is
built on—a mechanism-design result with a falsifiable cross-venue prediction
(Sec. 6). Read together, (iv) explains (iii): a cascade whose
multiplier never approaches unity has no diverging quantity for a pre-state
variable to track.

The remainder proceeds through data (Sec. 2), the four results, and
a synthesis (Sec. 7). The results are presented as a build
rather than in order of importance: the collective characterization first
(Sec. 3–4), then the branching model and its
elimination (Sec. 5), which is where λ\lambda is defined, and only
then the in-flight measurement of that same quantity (Sec. 6).
Two contemporaneous works frame ours:
Shukla et al. (2026) build high-frequency crypto interaction networks in
calm markets, a useful contrast to the in-cascade fabric studied here, and a
parallel preprint (rs9, 2025) compares CeFi and DeFi microstructure through
the same October 2025 event. We cite both as concurrent rather than antecedent.
